I have days when I can’t stop smiling, and others when I sit by the window and try to remember the sound of birds—sometimes I think I still hear them, faint and far away.

Take care of yourself, Marcus. Write if you can.
With all I have—
Clara

On Monday, Theo’s group revisited “The World’s Most Extraordinary Rats”. The children were fascinated, especially by—to my surprise—Joseph, who usually shies away from discussions about animals. Today, he stood up and asked, “Can rats learn to understand human words?” It reminded me of how you once described your rat, Lemon, tapping on her cage to communicate. I told the children about Lemon and how she “talked” to you. Suddenly, half the class wanted to invent a rat alphabet. Maybe we’ll build on that tomorrow.

Theo has been drawing the rat from “Temple of the Golden Rat” in his sketchbook, adding notes about how the rat wears a crown and carries a key to a secret door. He’s started making up stories about the rat’s adventures and wants to share them at show-and-tell. Mind you, he’s never volunteered for that before.

His confidence is growing, Elena. I see it in how he asks more questions, and in the way he listens—really listens—when others speak. He wants to understand the world, and every new fact is a secret key for him.

Last week, we learned about constellations and the story of Callisto. Theo asked if Greek myths explained why the sky looks the way it does. I told him that stories like Callisto’s helped people make sense of stars. He looked thoughtfully at the night sky chart and said, “Maybe every star has its own story.” I showed him how to find the Plough and the Little Dipper. He traced them with his finger, and for a moment, I could almost see the lines connecting his thoughts.

All these signs, big and small, remind me how deeply curious he is. The world still feels overwhelming at times, but now I see him building bridges between what he wonders and what he knows. 

Rest well, my friend. When you visit, I’ll save a seat under the oak for you, and I’ll have a fresh pot of rose tea waiting. And if Theo’s rat stories are any good, prepare yourself—he’s a natural storyteller now.

With warmth,
Daniel<|endoftext|>

Begin with Your Contact Information

[City, State, ZIP Code]

Dearest Marcus,

We have at last seen the last of the trunks and boxes laid to rest within our new abode. The kitchen is bathed in a fine, golden morning light, yet it seems less bright for your absence. I made an attempt at your cherished stew last evening, though it lacked that certain warmth which your careful hand always imparted to the pot.

Dear Archie,

Your letter found me on a damp and blustery London morning, the kind that makes one long for the golden light of Provence and, more importantly, the company of friends. Thank you for your warm invitation and your trust in my paltry talents with a frozen spoon. I would not miss this dinner for the world, nor would I let you serve a subpar sorbet to Claudia’s lamb.

Enclosed you’ll find the recipe I promised—a lemon-thyme sorbet with a whisper of honey to round out the bright notes. It’s simple but elegant, perfectly matched for a spring evening.

**Archie’s Lemon-Thyme Sorbet**  

*Ingredients:*  
- 3 large lemons (zested and juiced, about ¾ cup fresh juice)  
- 1 cup water  
- ¾ cup honey  
- ¼ cup fresh thyme leaves  
- 2 teaspoons lemon zest  
- 1½ cups cold water (for melting stage)  
- Pinch of sea salt  

*Instructions:*  
1. In a saucepan, combine the lemon juice, water, honey, and thyme. Bring just to a simmer, then remove from heat.  
2. Steep for 20 minutes, then strain out the thyme.  
3. Stir in the lemon zest and sea salt. Let the syrup cool to room temperature.  
4. Stir in the 1½ cups of cold water until dissolved.  
5. Pour the mixture into an ice cream maker and churn until thick and sorbetty.  
6. Once set, scrape into a chilled bowl and let it rest in the freezer for an hour before serving.  

I know you prefer things done simply, so this requires no fancy gadgets beyond the ice cream maker (I hope you still have that relic from Julia?). Serve in bowls with a sprinkle of thyme leaves and a slice of lemon atop.

I arrive tomorrow afternoon—don’t let Brooke tempt you into using frozen grapes as a shortcut! I look forward to seeing you both, to laughter, and to the gentle hush of your new kitchen filled with friends.

May the taste of summer linger on our tongues.  

Yours always,  
Marcus<|endoftext|>

Dear Marcus,
We unpacked the last box yesterday. The new kitchen gets lovely morning light, and
512.completion:
cooks much better than I expected given the wonky placement of the stove. And there are cupboards. I can’t stop touching the cupboards, nor tasting the tap water, nor saying “our new place” as if it has existed for years rather than weeks. It’s oddly thrilling, and also problematic, because I’m in an acute state of sensory overload I’m not sure how to metabolise. Partly because so many of the memories that came with the boxes are still a little too raw - it’s like the trauma of packing, moving and generally being homeless has saturated things with additional emotional significance. And that’s all fine because it’s necessary to let the grief breathe. Except that I’m also so certain that solid ground is the best place for that breathing. But the solid ground doesn’t quite feel solid yet.

It’s like all those conversations we had about urban memory that culminate in the question of how you can live in a place and have that place really live in you. I’m trying to decide whether this is that thing, or whether it’s another disjointed live-aboard experience. I’m swaying between a feeling of monumental inadequacy - I’m not designed for a life on land, I’ll never be competent here - and flourishes of domestic luxury - I’ll make coffee every morning and read and teach online and maybe even keep plants alive in pots. Isn’t that what we both wanted?

I wanted to tell you this as it feels like the beginning of something, and also a sequel to something, and also entirely abstract and meaningless. I still have no idea how I feel. But anyway. I am here. I can see you from that window sometimes, when your building turns just the right way with the light. I wonder if you can see me. I’m off to put the kettle on.
​ 
(from "Our New Place" by CB, published in The White Review, Issue 34, 2021. Used with permission).

Tips for Choosing a Closing Line
Match the Tone: Make sure the closing line fits the overall tone of your message. A professional report needs a formal close, while a friendly email allows something warmer.
Consider the Relationship: Use more personal closings with colleagues you know well; keep it formal with new contacts or clients.
Reflect the Purpose: If your message solved a problem or answered a question, affirm that with your closing (e.g., "We're glad we could help").
Teach Your Team: If you're writing on behalf of an organization, offer consistency by creating a list of approved closing lines that anyone can use.
Review for Consistency: If you're sending out a series of messages (like a newsletter), try to use similar closing styles to create brand recognition and familiarity.
By thoughtfully selecting your closing lines, you give your messages lasting impact and make sure they are remembered for the right reasons.
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) About Closing Lines
What is the difference between a closing line and a sign-off?
A closing line is the last sentence before your signature or sign-off that summarizes or leaves an impression. The sign-off (e.g., "Sincerely,") is what follows the body and precedes your name. For example:
I appreciate your help with this project.  
Sincerely,  
Jordan
